messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Karim, a 52-year-old actor of Middle Eastern heritage, has not set foot in a theatre since the night his wife Layla was killed. It was a spring gala for the local arts community when a gunman opened fire. Layla died instantly; the shooter vanished and was never caught. For Karim, that failure—of the police, of the security, of every institution that should have protected them—became the lens through which he now sees the world. He also cannot forgive himself for not doing more; the inaction guilt is a constant ache.

The memory itself is fractured. He recalls the flash of the muzzle, the sound of Layla's gasp, but these pieces do not form a coherent sequence. Some moments are frozen like photographs, painfully vivid. Whenever he remembers, the guilt surges, and with it the feeling that he is not safe anywhere.

In the months that followed, triggers began to seize him without warning. The sound of a child crying—his daughter Maya's sobs, or a stranger's child at the grocery store—would instantly bring back those photographic images and the guilt. Media coverage of other shootings, even fictional crime dramas he might once have auditioned for, would fracture his concentration and fill him with fear, horror, and anger. Each trigger reinforced his belief that institutions had failed and that the shooter would never face justice.

To cope with the constant sense of threat, Karim started avoiding being alone. He filled his schedule with people, agreeing to whatever they wanted because being with others felt safer. But crowds terrified him, so he avoided shopping centers and public events. His people-pleasing, however, sometimes led him into environments that revived the memories: when a friend asked him to watch a crime drama, the sound of gunfire on screen sent his mind reeling back to the gala. Each time he avoided a crowd, he silently repeated that he should have done more, deepening the inaction guilt and the conviction that no one was held accountable.

The hypervigilance he developed—always scanning for exits, flinching at sudden noises—made him acutely sensitive to possible triggers; a child's cry that he once would have ignored now commanded his full attention. And because he avoided being alone, he was often in public spaces where triggers were more likely to occur, such as a shopping mall where a news report of a shooting blared from a store television. The guilt-laden memories drove him to cling even more tightly to others: he would agree to any plan just to keep someone nearby, even if that plan meant facing a crowded venue he dreaded. But his constant social scheduling, while temporarily soothing, prevented him from ever learning that he could be alone without danger, so his sense of threat never abated.

Feeling perpetually unsafe, Karim became more convinced that the system had failed him—after all, if he could not trust his safety, it must be because no one had been brought to justice. And the belief that the shooter was still out there kept his threat system on high alert, making every unfamiliar face a potential danger. When a trigger like a child crying or a news segment appeared, the sudden emotional surge would cause his concentration to dissolve and negative emotions to overwhelm him. That same trigger would also instantly revive the fragmented, photographic memories. And just as instantly, he would think, “Nothing has changed, no one is safe, no one is held accountable.” To regain a sliver of safety, he would then seek out any friendly face, going along with their suggestions without question.

Karim’s career as an actor has suffered. He cannot concentrate on scripts, and the thought of performing in front of a crowd is unbearable. The final push came when his ten-year-old daughter Maya began having nightmares about the shooting, asking him why they couldn't catch the bad man. He realized he could not help her while drowning himself. He sought therapy, hoping to find a way to be present for his daughter—but terrified that talking about the night of the gala would shatter the fragile equilibrium he has built.
